content:
Inflammation is the body's natural response to injury or infection, causing heat, redness, swelling and pain. In inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, the immune system wrongly triggers this response in the joints and it keeps going, which can damage them. Osteoarthritis involves much less inflammation. Inflammatory arthritis needs specialist treatment with medicines that calm the immune system.

Inflammation: helpful and harmful

Short-term inflammation is protective. When you sprain an ankle, extra blood flow and immune cells help repair the damage, and the swelling settles. In inflammatory arthritis, inflammation becomes long-term and is directed at healthy tissue. The joint lining (synovium) thickens and produces extra fluid, causing swelling and pain. Over time it can wear away cartilage and bone.

Types of arthritis where inflammation is the main driver

  • rheumatoid arthritis
  • psoriatic arthritis
  • axial spondyloarthritis, including ankylosing spondylitis
  • gout, where crystals trigger sudden intense inflammation
  • lupus and other connective tissue diseases
  • reactive arthritis
  • polymyalgia rheumatica, which mainly affects muscles around the shoulders and hips

What about osteoarthritis?

Osteoarthritis was once seen as simple "wear and tear". We now know it involves the joint working to repair itself, with some low-grade inflammation. Joints may swell at times, particularly during a flare. However, the inflammation is much milder and is not driven by the immune system in the same way, so osteoarthritis is not treated with immune-suppressing medicines.

Signs of inflammatory arthritis

  • swollen, warm joints
  • stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes after waking or resting
  • pain that eases with movement
  • tiredness and feeling generally unwell
  • symptoms in several joints, often on both sides

If you notice these, see your GP. Early treatment protects joints.

How inflammation is measured

Blood tests can show inflammation. The most common are:

  • CRP (C-reactive protein)
  • ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate)

These are not specific to arthritis, as infections and other conditions raise them too. Some people with active inflammatory arthritis have normal results, so doctors also rely on examining your joints. Ultrasound can show inflammation in the joint lining.

Treatments that calm inflammation

  • NSAIDs (anti-inflammatory painkillers) reduce pain and swelling but do not change the disease. They are not suitable for everyone, so check with your pharmacist or GP.
  • Steroids work quickly and are often used for flares or short periods.
  • DMARDs such as methotrexate reduce immune activity and prevent damage. NICE recommends starting them early in RA.
  • Biologics and targeted therapies act on specific inflammatory signals when DMARDs are not enough.

Lifestyle and inflammation

Lifestyle changes cannot replace medicines for inflammatory arthritis, but they support your treatment and general health:

  • stop smoking, which worsens RA and can reduce how well treatment works
  • stay active, as regular exercise has anti-inflammatory effects
  • keep to a healthy weight, because fat tissue produces inflammatory chemicals
  • eat a balanced diet, such as a Mediterranean-style diet rich in vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, oily fish and olive oil
  • sleep well and manage stress

Be wary of products marketed as "anti-inflammatory cures". Supplements can interact with arthritis medicines, so check with your pharmacist first.

Living with inflammatory arthritis

With modern treatment, many people get their inflammation under control. Regular reviews with your rheumatology team, reporting flares promptly and keeping up with blood tests all help keep it that way.

Questions to ask your team

  • Is my arthritis inflammatory, and how active is it?
  • What do my CRP and ESR results mean for me?
  • How will we know if treatment is working?
  • What should I do if I notice new swelling?

Understanding your own results helps you spot changes early and take part in decisions about your care.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
